title: EDUCATION | 5.25.26 The Inherent Challenge of Teaching a Class of Individuals – Who Each Matter Equally: A Thought Experiment
author: Sherrington, Tom
summary: A thought experiment exposes a structural gap at the heart of classroom teaching: if a teacher had only one student—the least confident in the class—they would interact continuously, track every uncertainty, and never let a learning gap go unaddressed. But when thirty students rejoin the room, none of those individual needs change; what changes is the structural reality of group instruction. It becomes entirely possible for that student to sit through an entire lesson without a single direct engagement from the teacher—and the teacher may not even notice. The student does notice, but because it is their norm, they simply accept it. The article frames this as a brutal reality check: the system's default is to call on volunteers and assume others are following, without any meaningful monitoring of individual progress. Truly inclusive teaching is not the emergent result of caring; it requires deliberate, systematic strategies that structurally involve every learner in every lesson. The key questions every teacher must hold: is there anyone in the room struggling in silence, and how would I even know?
points: * A thought experiment shows that adding 29 students to a one-on-one interaction does not change any individual student's needs—but completely transforms what a teacher can structurally do for them. * It is entirely possible for the least-confident student to experience a full lesson with zero direct engagement from the teacher, while the teacher remains unaware this has happened. * The student accepts this invisibility as normal—their norm—while the teacher's attention flows to volunteers and visible participation. * The system default is not inclusive: it selects from volunteers and assumes others are following, without any teacher knowing how a given individual is actually doing. * Truly inclusive teaching must be deliberately and systematically designed through whole-class techniques; good intentions alone do not produce it.
quotes: With only one student, you would interact with them continually, tuning into how well they're responding to the instruction, noticing successes, uncertainties, errors, gaps in knowledge, subtle issues in their performance.

In fact it might be possible for there to be no direct engagement between that original student and the teacher at all for a whole lesson – and the teacher doesn't even notice. But the student does (except that it's their norm so they don't actually think about it.).

The reflection point for any teacher is: could it be possible to sit in your lesson and feel that the lesson is going on around you but that you're not in it; that you're just one of many lumped together without your own learning gaps surfacing and being addressed?

I would say, with some confidence, that across the system, truly inclusive teaching is not the default; the default is to select volunteers or individuals and assume that others are listening, following, hanging in there, without the teacher knowing how they're doing in any meaningful sense.

The truth is that the gap between how that student experiences the full class lesson and what they'd experience on their own is potentially vast – unless, teachers explicitly deliberately adopt inclusive teaching strategies at all times.
